faqs.question: What size should a Ganesh Chaturthi logo be?
faqs.answer: There is no single size, which is the point of drawing it as a vector. Design it so it still reads at about 40 pixels — that is the size a group icon is actually displayed at — and it will scale up to a twenty-foot arch without redrawing. If you need a fixed export, a 1024x1024 PNG with transparency covers almost every digital use.

faqs.question: Why does my Ganesh Chaturthi logo look fine in the editor but bad as a WhatsApp group icon?
faqs.answer: Two things happen at once: it shrinks, and it gets cropped to a circle. Thin strokes fill in and any two shapes closer together than the stroke thickness merge into one blob, while the circular mask removes the corners — a plain inscribed circle keeps only 78.5% of a square. Test at 40 pixels inside a circle before you finalise anything.

faqs.question: Can I put my mandal's name inside the logo?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only in the large version. Keep two locked files: a full lockup with the symbol, mandal name and year for the arch, banner, letterhead and receipt header, and a symbol-only icon with no words for the group photo, the stamp and anything under roughly 100 pixels.

faqs.question: Does a Ganesh Chaturthi logo need to work in black and white?
faqs.answer: It does, because receipt books, rubber stamps and duplicate slips are normally printed in one ink. Build the single-colour version first as pure black on white with no tints or gradients, then add colour on top. Android takes the same position as a hard requirement: supporting themed app icons means shipping a single monochrome layer.

faqs.question: How much does losing the colour actually cost?
faqs.answer: Measurably little. In a 2009 experiment on objects whose identity is tied to a colour, naming took 891 ms in the correct colour and 923 ms in greyscale — about 32 ms. The wrong colour cost 986 ms, roughly three times the greyscale penalty, so a mismatched print is worse than a one-ink print.

faqs.question: Should the logo be simple or detailed?
faqs.answer: Simple, but for a specific reason. A 2022 study found visual complexity — the count of lines and closed figures in an icon — did not significantly change whether people understood it, while concreteness did, with a large effect. So keep one recognisable thing, a trunk, a modak or a durva sprig, and strip the rest.

faqs.question: What is the safe zone for a circular logo crop?
faqs.answer: Android's adaptive icon spec guarantees a 66x66 safe zone centred inside a 108x108 container — 61% of the width, or about 37% of the drawn area — as the region no manufacturer's mask will ever clip. Masks vary by handset, from a circle to a squircle, so anything outside that centre is not guaranteed to survive.

faqs.question: Is an AI logo maker good enough for a mandal?
faqs.answer: It will give you an image, not an identity. A generator optimises what you see at full size and has no mechanism to check the mark at 40 pixels, in one ink, or inside a circle — which are the three things that decide whether a mandal can reuse it next year. If you use one, run all three tests on the output yourself.

faqs.question: Do I need a different logo for the arch and for the group icon?
faqs.answer: Not a different logo — a different lockup of the same mark. One symbol, two arrangements: symbol plus name plus year for large formats, symbol alone for small ones. If the two need different symbols, the symbol is too complicated.

faqs.question: What file formats should the mandal keep?
faqs.answer: Keep an editable vector as the master, since that is what lets one mark serve a phone screen and large-format signage from the same file. Export a transparent PNG at 1024 pixels for digital use, and a one-colour black version for the printer. Hand all three to whoever runs the mandal next year.

faqs.question: When should we not bother with a logo at all?
faqs.answer: If the mandal will not reuse the mark, skip it. The reproduction discipline only pays back when the same mark reappears — on next year's receipt book, next year's arch, the same group icon. For a one-off celebration, commission the banner artwork instead and spend the time on the pandal.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganesh Chaturthi Logo Design: One Mark for 200 Pixels, One Colour and a Twenty-Foot Arch

A Ganesh Chaturthi logo design is not artwork — it is an identity mark that has to be the *same* mark on a WhatsApp group icon, on a receipt book printed in one colour, and on a twenty-foot pandal arch. Nearly every page ranking for this phrase hands over a vector file and stops. What decides whether that file works is reproduction: what survives shrinking, what survives having the colour taken out, and what survives a circular crop. The small end matters most, and the platform data says why. Across 46,005 recorded views of shared pages on SubhSandesh, 49.6% of shared pages are opened on a phone (22,817 of 46,005 views), and 49.8% of views are on a touch device (phone or tablet). So the mark spends most of its life a few centimetres wide, in a thumbnail, in someone's hand. Design it for that and the arch takes care of itself.

## What a logo has to do that a banner does not

A banner is one file at one size, used once. A mandal logo is one mark reused across a group icon, a donation receipt, volunteer T-shirts, the aarti schedule taped to a pole, and the arch — five surfaces, four printers, ten days.

That reuse is the whole difference, and it changes the brief. A banner can carry detail because you know exactly how far away it will be read, so its brief reduces to millimetres of cap height at a stated viewing distance. A mark cannot know its final size, so it has to hold up across every size it might land at.

There is a useful precedent in how research-grade icons are built. When a 2022 study in *Displays* designed 64 icons to test what makes an icon understood, it drew every one on a 24×24 vector grid with a single grid square as the stroke width, in black and white only, as vectors — explicitly so the icons could be shown anywhere "from retina screens to large-scale signage systems". That is the same problem a mandal has.

## The three reproductions one mark has to survive

### 1. The group icon, roughly 200 pixels, cropped to a circle

This is where the mark is smallest and seen most. It gets displayed at a fraction of its file size, masked into a circle, next to nineteen other group icons in a list.

### 2. The one-colour print run — receipt books, stamps, slips

Donation receipts, rubber stamps and duplicate books are usually printed in a single ink because it is cheap and fast. Gradients, glows and drop shadows do not exist there. Neither does the difference between your saffron and your gold.

### 3. The arch, the flex, the stage backdrop

Here the mark is enormous and viewed from far away, which is the easy case for size and the hard case for craft. Every soft edge and stray anchor point in the vector becomes visible at two metres tall.

A mark that works at all three is not the average of three designs. It is the one design that clears the hardest constraint each surface imposes — and the constraints are specific enough to test before you commit.

## The shrink test: what disappears first

Shrink the mark to 40 pixels and look at what merges. Thin strokes fill in, gaps between strokes close, and any two shapes closer together than the stroke is thick become one shape.

The 2022 *Displays* study is unusually helpful here because it separated two things designers usually conflate. Visual complexity — measured as the raw count of lines, closed figures, open figures and letters in the mark — did **not** significantly affect whether people understood what an icon meant (F < 1). What did was concreteness: recognisably concrete icons were understood significantly more accurately than abstract ones, F(1, 63) = 23.40, p < .001, with a large effect size of η²p = .30.

Read practically, that is permission to strip. Detail is not what makes your mark legible; a recognisable thing is. A trunk, a modak, a durva sprig or a single lotus in clean silhouette will read at 40 pixels. Eleven overlapping motifs will not, and the study also found simple icons were rated more appealing than complex ones, F(1, 56) = 4.03, p = .05.

## Single colour: what is left when the colour is taken out

Every mandal logo will eventually be printed in one ink, and the honest question is how much that costs. There is a measured answer, from a 2009 experiment in *Cognitive Processing* on objects whose identity is strongly tied to a colour.

Naming those objects took 891 ms in their correct colour, 923 ms in greyscale, and 986 ms in the wrong colour — every gap statistically significant. So removing the colour cost about 32 ms. Printing it in the *wrong* colour cost three times as much, 95 ms against the correct version.

That is the useful ratio. Greyscale is a small, real penalty; a mark whose meaning depends on a colour that the printer cannot match is a much bigger one. Android makes the same point as a requirement rather than a finding: to support themed icons, an app must supply a **single monochrome layer** of its icon alongside the colour version.

So build the one-colour version first, as pure black on white with no tints, and treat colour as something added on top. If the mark still reads with the colour gone, it will read on the receipt book, the stamp, the fax-quality photocopy and the embroidered cap.

## The circular crop, and how much it takes

Circular crops are not a rounding error. Android's adaptive icon spec guarantees only a **66×66 safe zone centred inside a 108×108 container** — the area "never clipped by a shaped mask defined by an OEM", where the mask may be a circle on one handset and a squircle on another.

Do the arithmetic and that safe zone is 61% of the width and about **37% of the drawn area**. Even a plain circle inscribed in a square keeps only π/4, or 78.5%, of the square — the corners lose 21.5% before any platform gets involved.

The practical rule follows: nothing that identifies the mark may sit in the corners, and the mark's silhouette should be roughly as tall as it is wide. Marks built on a wide horizontal lockup — name to the right of a symbol — lose their name to the crop every time, which is why the icon version is usually the symbol alone.

## Where the mandal's name goes, and when it drops out

Most searches behind this keyword are really about a group name, not a symbol: the mandal, the gully, the year, sometimes all three. That text is the first casualty of every constraint above.

Draw two locked files instead of arguing about it. The full lockup — symbol plus name plus year — is for the arch, the banner, the letterhead and the receipt header. The icon-only version, symbol with no words at all, is for the group photo, the stamp and anywhere under about 100 pixels.

The 2001 *Journal of Consumer Research* study of brand logo complexity found in its own pretest that familiar logos were rated significantly simpler than novel ones (M = 3.06 versus M = 4.66, F(1, 702) = 187.5, p < .01). Its authors argued complexity is largely a red herring: what makes a mark process easily is uniformity along a single structural dimension, plus consistent meaning. A mandal already has both to hand — one silhouette, one story, repeated for ten days.

## The three reproductions, side by side

| Surface | Typical size | Colours available | What must be readable | Platform share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Group icon / shared page | ~200 px, circle-cropped | Full colour, plus a mono version | Symbol silhouette only | 49.6% of 46,005 views are on a phone |
| Receipt book, stamp, slip | 15–40 mm | One ink | Symbol, and the name if set large | Not measured — offline surface |
| Arch, flex, backdrop | 1–6 m | Full colour | Symbol, name, year | 0 of 46,005 measured views |

The last column is the honest part. SubhSandesh has data on the digital surface and none at all on the printed ones, because it has never printed anything.

## Where a logo is the wrong thing to make

If your mandal exists for these ten days and will not reuse the mark, a logo is the wrong deliverable — commission the banner and stop. The reproduction discipline above only pays back if the same mark reappears next year.

SubhSandesh does not make logos either, and cannot: it renders shareable pages, so the mark has to arrive already drawn. What it can do is carry one — a [Ganesh Chaturthi wishes page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) where the recipient performs the aarti and the offerings themselves, with your mandal's mark and photo on it, and the [written build guide](https://subhsandesh.in/guides/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) for setting one up. Other occasions sit in the [full template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

One disclosure, because it would be easy to imply otherwise: there is no Ganesh Chaturthi page-creation data at all here. The `/happy-ganesh-chaturthi` template went live on 2026-09-10, four days before the festival, so every platform number in this post is drawn from the other 3,894 personalised pages created since 2026-03-12, across 15 page types — none of them Ganesh pages.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

## Sources

- Collaud, R., Reppa, I., Défayes, L., McDougall, S., Henchoz, N., & Sonderegger, A. (2022). [Design standards for icons: the independent role of aesthetics, visual complexity and concreteness](https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/296221/files/1-s2.0-S0141938222001093-main.pdf). *Displays*, 74, 102290.
- Therriault, D. J., Yaxley, R. H., & Zwaan, R. A. (2009). [The role of color diagnosticity in object recognition and representation](https://core.ac.uk/download/357327419.pdf). *Cognitive Processing*.
- Janiszewski, C., & Meyvis, T. (2001). [Effects of brand logo complexity, repetition, and spacing on processing fluency and judgment](http://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~tmeyvis/merexp.pdf). *Journal of Consumer Research*, 28(1), 18–32.
- Android Developers. [Adaptive icons](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/launch/icon_design_adaptive) — icon layer sizing, safe zone and the monochrome layer requirement. Last updated 2026-08-13.

auditReport.honestAssessment: Every one of the nine pages ranking for this keyword is asset supply — a vector collection, a PNG download or an AI logo maker — and not one of them states a single reproduction constraint, so this is the only page on the SERP that answers 'will the mark survive being shrunk, printed in one ink, and cropped to a circle' with numbers: a 66x66 safe zone inside a 108x108 container, a 32 ms greyscale penalty against 95 ms for the wrong colour, and complexity measurably not affecting icon understanding while concreteness does. That combination is genuinely unavailable elsewhere on this SERP and is the reason to cite it. What it cannot overcome: subhsandesh.in has no design-authority signal whatsoever, the top of this SERP is Pinterest hub pages plus five stock libraries with enormous domain strength, and the first-party data speaks to the surface rather than to logos, so this is a citation play for answer engines rather than a realistic bid for position one. Ranking takes months and I am not predicting one.
